gap: None of the results ChatGPT got gives an independently measured figure for how much energy a Jackery actually delivers. GearLab's light-bulb load jig got 910 Wh of AC out of the Explorer 1000 v2, which is rated at 1,070 Wh (85%), and 1,710 Wh out of the Explorer 2000 v2, rated at 2,042 Wh (84%). nextpit got 902 Wh and 1,920 Wh from the same two models and only 237 Wh from the 288 Wh 300 Plus.
standout_why: Compared against all nine results ChatGPT got. GearBrain's HomePower 1000 Plus V2 piece (dated 2026-08-28) says it 'has not yet conducted hands-on testing' and lists only Jackery's claims. 10adventures tested the old Explorer 500 and gives no measured Wh, efficiency or noise. TechRadar's IP65 item and both Notebookcheck pieces (Explorer 1500 Ultra, Explorer 1000 v2) are launch or news stories by their titles; I did not open them. ProToolReviews returned HTTP 403, and its search title, 'Jackery Drops Its Most Outdoor-Ready Portable Power Station Yet', reads as launch news. I also did not open REI (a store listing), jackery.com (the maker's own blog) or Yahoo (a deal story). None of the result titles points to a measured output, efficiency or noise figure.
decides: This confirms the pick rather than changing it. Two independent testers got 84–88% of rated capacity from the 1000 v2 and the 2000 v2, so a shopper should plan around about 900 Wh and about 1,700–1,900 Wh of AC energy, not the numbers on the label. The small 300 Plus loses proportionally more: nextpit got 237 of 288 Wh and 72% round trip. That favours moving up to the 1000 v2 for anything beyond phones and laptops. I found no measured output for the 1500 Ultra, so it can't be ranked on delivered energy.
